subject: Model Fit Indices -  Hows my model?

messages.author: fdc70beaef2da0e2
messages.subject: Model Fit Indices -  Hows my model?
parts:
Dear all,

I am running a CLPM in Lavaan, to explore a possible bidirectional association between two variables, measured at two time points. Its part of a longitudinal study. I include ~3300 children in this specific analysis and adjust for covariates in 3 incremental steps/models. 

However, I have doubts on the accuracy of my model. CFI, RMSEA and SRMR seem good. However, my Chi-square is quite large. This is where I'd like your input. Some argue that in large samples (does mine qualify as large, for such a statement?) even small and substantively unimportant differences between the estimated model and the ‘true’ underlying model will result in rejection of the model that is tested. Do you guys think I should reject my model or do you think it seems fine?

My fit indices are as follows:



Thank you in advance! 

Best.

messages.author: edceb8dce9472a62
messages.subject: Re: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
parts:
Hello, 

This certainly is a large enough sample to magnify a small amount of misfit based on your sample size, but that is a large chi square... 
Your other fit indices are good, but 'how good' depends on the importance of your research question. In my opinion, these are decent fit indices and I wouldn't think twice if this were for anything less than publication. Given a few persistent researchers are stubborn about significant chi-square, I would try and better fit the model to the data if I were publishing. Without a third wave to try an RICLPM model, I'm not sure how you would do that, however.

If this isn't your cup of tea, you can do some research on Hoelter's N, which was invented to tell you what number of participants would make your model's chi square significant (because power works "against you" in SEM). if you call fitmeasures(model_fit, "cn_05"), you will get a number for your model at p = 0.05 significance level. A rule of thumb (used by Hoelter, at least) was 200+ indicates it's "okay" that your chi square is significant (with ML or MLR), but I have not personally found a simulation study of the exact number. Either way, it's "not interpretable" when chi-square isn't significant, according to many. I want to point out that some very well respected researchers (e.g., Hu & Bentler) do not recommend using this, however. 

For more information about what specific fit indices should be, you should think about what the formula for that index is, for example RMSEA is fit (or misfit) per df, so (for example) RMSEA is often artificially better in models with large numbers of df than other models. More information on both can be found and easily interpreted here (http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm)

As an aside, this is mainly a forum for technical questions about lavaan, not general SEM questions, even if it gets used as both. But, admittedly, I have been the guy asking general SEM questions before, which is why I took the time to answer this one and free up time of the smarter minds of Yves and Terrence, haha).

Best,
Chris

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
parts:
Hi

As mentioned before, the RMSEA is a misfit per df, and in your models you have a lot of df to disperse it across. This is why RMSEA will tend to prefer larger models. Previous research has showns that CFI and Gamma-Hat are probably the best fit indices at being less sensitive to other sample/model characterictics. You can get gamma-hat from the moreFitIndices() function in semTools

Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864

Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224

On the other side, these are overall model fit evaluation, which has the limitation of possibly missed local misfit. So, after having "good" overall model fit you should also look at residuals and modification indices to evaluate if there is the need to add parameters to account for local misfit. The SRMR is the average bias in the residual correlations, so there might be some misfit related to specific items

Whittaker, T. A. (2012). Using the Modification Index and Standardized Expected Parameter Change for Model Modification. The Journal of Experimental Education, 80(1), 26–44. https://doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2010.531299

Related to sample size and the chi-square, I am on the side that as a Null Hypothesis Significance Test (NHST), the chi square is designed to reject models with small amounts of misfit as sample size increases, so I in general dont pay attention too much to it.

Also, about the other fit indices (absolute, relative, or residuals), they were not designed to "accept" or "reject" a model like a NHST, they were designed as effect size metrics of misfit of the model (evaluated in different ways). But it has fallen into the common (bad) practice of using them as a NHST of "is a good model", but they should be answering "how much if the misfit of my model to represent the data?". On the same direction, the commonly used cutoffs for fit indices are not recommended as the recommended cutoffs come from specific research that does not allow to generalize them

Hope this helps

parts:
Dear Mauricio,

This very much helps, indeed! Thank you for taking the time to comment. Greatly appreciated.

df is high because I am using 4 latent variables, for 2 constructs at 2 time points. Variable A is measured using the same 2 items at 10 and 14 years. Variable B is measured using the same 7 items at 10 and 14 years. All the items are ordered. 

This is the unadjusted model I am currently using:
Model1.0 <- '

# Latent variables age 10
VariableA_10 =~ ItemA1_10 + ItemA2_10
VariableB_10 =~ ItemB1_10 + ItemB2_10 + ItemB3_10 + ItemB4_10 + ItemB5_10 + ItemB6_10 + ItemB7_10

# Latent variables age 14
VariableA_14 =~ ItemA1_14 + ItemA2_14
VariableB_14 =~ ItemB1_14 + ItemB2_14 + ItemB3_14 + ItemB4_14 + ItemB5_14 + ItemB6_14 + ItemB7_14

# Regressions:
VariableA_14 ~ VariableA_10 + VariableB_10
VariableB_14 ~ VariableB_10 + VariableA_10

# Covariances
VariableA_10 ~~ VariableB_10
'

Based on the modification indices and residuals, there indeed seems to be some local misfit. 
For example modificationindices(mymodelfit.model1.0, sort.= TRUE, minimum.value = 20) returns:

                    lhs op           rhs      mi           epc     sepc.lv   sepc.all sepc.nox

291 ItemB6_10 ~~ ItemB6_14   166.243  0.325   0.325    0.482    0.482

255 ItemB3_10 ~~ ItemB6_14   109.582  0.224   0.224    0.536    0.536

320 ItemB1_14 ~~ ItemB5_14     87.652  0.154   0.154    0.768    0.768

337 ItemB6_14 ~~ ItemB7_14     80.766  0.241   0.241    0.433    0.433

283 ItemB6_10 ~~ ItemB7_10     77.666  0.257   0.257    0.468    0.468


Do you think I should correlate these measurement residuals or make any other adjustments to my model? I am hesitant to make post-hoc adjustments to the model. 

Thanks again! 

Best,

Joost

messages.subject: Re: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
parts:
Joost,

Those are some very large modification indices.

The first one. ItemB6_10 ~~ ItemB6_14, looks like the same item at two timepoints. It is usually not controversial to allow disturbance covariances in that situation, even if it is post hoc.

Further, most of the large residuals involve variable B6. Before making any changes, I suggest you check the residuals in your model to get a better grasp of what's going on with it.

And finally, and this will worsen fit, CLPMs usually impose metric invariance longitudinally. It's not clear what information you'll get out of this otherwise. I'm surprised the VariableA_14 portion of the model was identified without it.

Pat

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
parts:
Oh, Ok, its a panel model

I would recommend to look at these modifications on the measurement model, without regressions yet.

Also, in models like this is common to add all the disturbance covariances for the same item over time. This would be saying that there is something common between the same item over time that is above and beyond the relation between factors. Which is not hard to argue.

Next, if you were to still have large mi and spec.all, you should also have to consider if the modification makes theoretical sense and you can justify it? By adding a disturbance covariance, you are saying that there is something in common between those 2 indicators above and beyond the relations between factors, can you argue that for those added parameters. An issue with modification indices is that that can get out of control by adding parameters that would help the model but are not relevant. Remember SEM is a theory based approach, so by adding any modification you would be recommending future researchers to add those same parameters

If the items are ordered, are you treating them as such? Ans using WLS?

Op dinsdag 21 juli 2020 22:41:40 UTC+2 schreef Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal:
Hi

As mentioned before, the RMSEA is a misfit per df, and in your models you have a lot of df to disperse it across. This is why RMSEA will tend to prefer larger models. Previous research has showns that CFI and Gamma-Hat are probably the best fit indices at being less sensitive to other sample/model characterictics. You can get gamma-hat from the moreFitIndices() function in semTools

Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864

Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224

On the other side, these are overall model fit evaluation, which has the limitation of possibly missed local misfit. So, after having "good" overall model fit you should also look at residuals and modification indices to evaluate if there is the need to add parameters to account for local misfit. The SRMR is the average bias in the residual correlations, so there might be some misfit related to specific items

Whittaker, T. A. (2012). Using the Modification Index and Standardized Expected Parameter Change for Model Modification. The Journal of Experimental Education, 80(1), 26–44. https://doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2010.531299

Related to sample size and the chi-square, I am on the side that as a Null Hypothesis Significance Test (NHST), the chi square is designed to reject models with small amounts of misfit as sample size increases, so I in general dont pay attention too much to it.

Also, about the other fit indices (absolute, relative, or residuals), they were not designed to "accept" or "reject" a model like a NHST, they were designed as effect size metrics of misfit of the model (evaluated in different ways). But it has fallen into the common (bad) practice of using them as a NHST of "is a good model", but they should be answering "how much if the misfit of my model to represent the data?". On the same direction, the commonly used cutoffs for fit indices are not recommended as the recommended cutoffs come from specific research that does not allow to generalize them

Hope this helps

Hello, 

This certainly is a large enough sample to magnify a small amount of misfit based on your sample size, but that is a large chi square... 
Your other fit indices are good, but 'how good' depends on the importance of your research question. In my opinion, these are decent fit indices and I wouldn't think twice if this were for anything less than publication. Given a few persistent researchers are stubborn about significant chi-square, I would try and better fit the model to the data if I were publishing. Without a third wave to try an RICLPM model, I'm not sure how you would do that, however.

If this isn't your cup of tea, you can do some research on Hoelter's N, which was invented to tell you what number of participants would make your model's chi square significant (because power works "against you" in SEM). if you call fitmeasures(model_fit, "cn_05"), you will get a number for your model at p = 0.05 significance level. A rule of thumb (used by Hoelter, at least) was 200+ indicates it's "okay" that your chi square is significant (with ML or MLR), but I have not personally found a simulation study of the exact number. Either way, it's "not interpretable" when chi-square isn't significant, according to many. I want to point out that some very well respected researchers (e.g., Hu & Bentler) do not recommend using this, however. 

For more information about what specific fit indices should be, you should think about what the formula for that index is, for example RMSEA is fit (or misfit) per df, so (for example) RMSEA is often artificially better in models with large numbers of df than other models. More information on both can be found and easily interpreted here (http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm)

As an aside, this is mainly a forum for technical questions about lavaan, not general SEM questions, even if it gets used as both. But, admittedly, I have been the guy asking general SEM questions before, which is why I took the time to answer this one and free up time of the smarter minds of Yves and Terrence, haha).
